metric: CPU time of the core (src/gcm.c and its envelope) relative to bare OpenSSL EVP AES-256-GCM of the same shape: the random seal and the open over the bare random seal and open, which draw a random nonce as the core's random seal does, and the deterministic seal over a bare deterministic seal with the same hand-rolled HMAC-SHA256 nonce derivation (spec 1.8)
gate: for each size, the seal and open ratios (the core over bare EVP) and the det ratio (the core's deterministic seal over a bare deterministic seal of the same shape) must be at most the matching ceiling; the core's deterministic seal over its random one is recorded, never gated
note: A ratio, never nanoseconds, so it is portable across runners. Each benchmark runs five times in a random order and the gate reads the median of the raw repetitions. The ceilings are per size because the core's fixed per-call cost is a larger share of a small message; sizes live in tests/bench/benchmark.cc (kSizes). Both sides of det pay the same two HMAC-SHA256 computations (one over the label, one over be64(len(A)) || A || plaintext) and the same AES-GCM, so det is like-for-like whatever the runner's CPU accelerates. The deterministic seal over the random one is not like-for-like — it compares a SHA-256-bound seal with an AES-bound one — and an O17 probe found it ranging from about 1.2 to 9.6 across sizes, because AES-GCM and SHA-256 scale differently across runner CPU and libcrypto, so it is recorded, not gated. `recorded_ratios` holds the worst observed value per size over the three `main` runs of 2026-10-14, both libcryptos each, and `runner_cpu` the models they ran on; each ceiling is that worst value times 1.2 rounded up to one decimal (1.3 everywhere, 1.4 for the 256-byte seal) and no higher than the placeholder it replaced. Refresh the record and the ceilings the same way from three runs of `bench.yml` on `main` whenever the measured path changes.
